---
title: "A reverse-KL model of aesthetic preferences"
description: "An intrinsic reward for sampling individual perceptual-prior gradients."
---

::: {#key-ideas .callout-note title="Key ideas"}
- The intrinsic policy seeks individual latents that efficiently estimate the prior gradient under the extrinsic policy.
- A log gradient norm plus a log latent-frequency ratio gives a reward whose expectation minimizes reverse KL to the optimal single-latent proposal.
- Running feature averages from extrinsic experience can help estimate the ratio without fitting two latent densities.
:::

Unlike the [trajectory BPO candidate](computational-aesthetics.qmd), this
model treats one latent as the sampling unit. Let $p_{\pi_e}(z)$ and
$p_{\pi_i}(z)$ be the latent marginals under task and intrinsic behavior.
Use the same initial conditions and time weighting for both: for example,
draw one time step uniformly from a fixed-length trajectory. Hold the
encoder, extrinsic policy, and current prior fixed when comparing samplers.

## From a sampling distribution to a reward

The target loss and the gradient contributed by one latent are
$$
  L(\theta)=\mathbb E_{p_{\pi_e}}[-\log R_\theta(Z)],\qquad
  g_\theta(z)=\nabla_\theta[-\log R_\theta(z)].
$$
For a latent from an intrinsic trajectory the estimate is
$\widehat g(z)=w(z)g_\theta(z)$, with
$w(z)=p_{\pi_e}(z)/p_{\pi_i}(z)$. It is unbiased if the sampler covers every
region contributing to the target gradient. The unrestricted proposal minimizing
the sum of the component variances is [@alain2016, Theorem 1]
$$
  q_\theta^*(z)=p_{\pi_e}(z)\|g_\theta(z)\|_2/C_\theta,\qquad
  C_\theta=\mathbb E_{p_{\pi_e}}\|g_\theta(Z)\|_2.
$$
Assume $0<C_\theta<\infty$ and finite estimator second moments.

BPO uses forward KL from the optimal proposal to the behavioral distribution.
Reversing the arguments puts the expectation under the policy collecting the
reward. Assign each observed latent
$$
  r_I(z)=\log\|g_\theta(z)\|_2+\log w(z).
$$
Substituting $q_\theta^*$ gives
$$
  \mathbb E_{p_{\pi_i}}[r_I(Z)]
  =\log C_\theta-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{\pi_i}\Vert q_\theta^*).
$$
Thus maximizing expected reward fits the intrinsic latent marginal by reverse
KL. Coverage still requires a separate constraint: a policy can earn finite
reward while never visiting a contributing region. If the policy can realize
$q_\theta^*$ it attains the single-sample variance optimum. Otherwise a smaller
reverse KL need not imply smaller variance. Nor does the single-sample result
account for correlations among successive latents or measure actual learning
progress.

## Candidate estimator: running latent feature averages {#sec-feature-ema}

Least-squares importance fitting [@kanamori2009, sec. 2.2] estimates the
ratio directly by minimizing
$$
  \mathcal L(w)=\tfrac12\mathbb E_{p_{\pi_i}}[w(Z)^2]
                   -\mathbb E_{p_{\pi_e}}[w(Z)].
$$
When the target marginal is supported by the sampling marginal and the ratio
has finite second moment, this is half the mean squared ratio error under
$p_{\pi_i}$ up to an additive constant.

For $w_\eta(z)=\eta^\top f(z)$, maintain an exponential moving average $m_e$
of fixed features $f(z)$ **from extrinsic trajectories only**. Then
$\eta^\top m_e$ estimates the second expectation; intrinsic samples supply
the first. One-hot features retain category frequencies, whereas the mean of
a continuous latent alone cannot distinguish distributions with the same
mean but different tails.

On an intrinsic trajectory use the pre-update $w_\eta(z)$ twice: add its log
to the log gradient norm for the reward, and multiply $g_\theta(z)$ by it for
the prior update. Finite rewards require positive weights and gradient norms.
Flooring estimates can introduce bias. Limited features, correlated samples,
and policy drift may also compromise the estimate.
